Matsui Center for Politics & Public Service encompasses innovative student programming, internships, and experiential learning programs to provide opportunities and networks for outstanding students, nurturing a new and more diverse set of leaders for California and the nation.

November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.
Table Coding Key
Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.
Newspapers
Many newspapers require a subscription. Whenever possible, we link to a freely available version online. In other cases, we search Access World News, a UCB licensed database, to identify and link to endorsements. A current CalNet ID and password is required to access the articles.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

How this is built
Proposition 2 is forecast as a bonds and budgets measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. How this is built
Proposition 2 is forecast as a bonds and budgets measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. The following is a list of statewide measures that have qualified for the ballot. For those measures that are currently attempting to qualify, see the Initiative and Referendum Qualification Status (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status) page.
For initiative measures that are eligible for the ballot, see the Eligible Statewide Initiative Measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures) page. An eligible initiative measure is one in which the required number of signatures have been submitted to and verified by the county elections officials. Eligible initiative measures will become qualified for the ballot on the 131st day prior to the next Statewide General Election unless withdrawn by the proponents prior to its qualification by the Secretary of State.
For information on the campaign committees that have organized to support or oppose propositions and ballot measures on the statewide ballot, see the Propositions and Ballot Measures Campaign Finance Activity (http://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Measures/) page.
November 3, 2026, Statewide Ballot Measures
Proposition 1
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm)
Proposition 2
Increases State's Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm)
Proposition 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm)
Proposition 4
Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm)
Proposition 5

Proposition 37
Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm)
Proposition 38
Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm)
Proposition 39
Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm)
Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/index.htm)
Proposition 41
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/41/index.htm)
Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm)
Proposition 43
Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm)
Proposition 44
Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/index.htm)
Proposition 45
Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm)

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. Proposition 2
Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
The State Budget
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
How Does the State Raise Revenue? The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the General Fund. Other major taxes include the corporation tax and the sales tax. Much of the income tax is paid by high-income taxpayers, whose incomes often include gains from stocks and other investments.
State Revenues Are Unpredictable. State revenues go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because revenues depend on how the economy and stock market are doing. When things are going well, revenues can grow quickly. When things are going badly, like during a recession or a stock market crash, revenues can decline by tens of billions of dollars. During a bad recession or market crash, total revenue declines over a few years can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.
The State Must Meet Certain Budgeting Requirements Each Year. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget each year. This means the state cannot adopt a budget that spends more money than is available. In addition, the State Constitution limits how much tax revenue the state can spend. This limit is called the "state appropriations limit." Certain kinds of spending-like infrastructure-do not count toward the limit. All other spending, including money put into reserves, does count toward the limit.
Reserves
Reserves Allow the State to Maintain Spending When Revenues Decline. The state puts money into reserves when the economy is doing well. This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time. When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs. Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget. Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the "Rainy Day Fund." The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state's main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year. Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program. In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal. During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level. Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits. The money that would have gone into the rainy day fund instead must be spent on infrastructure (like highways and housing).
Debt
The State Has Different Kinds of Debts. The state has more than $250 billion in debts. These include debt for infrastructure and pension and retiree health benefits earned by state employees. The state also sometimes borrows money from other state funds to help pay General Fund costs. State debts are repaid over time, usually according to a schedule or plan. Each year, the state makes payments toward its debts.
State Constitution Requires the State to Make Extra Debt Payments Toward Pension and Health Benefits. The State Constitution requires the state to make extra debt payments above those normally made each year. The amount of these extra debt payments is the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. The state may only use these extra debt payments to pay down long-term pension and retiree health care debts. Making extra payments toward these debts saves the state money in the long run.
Extra Debt Payments Optional After 2030. The requirement for extra debt payments ends in 2030. After that, the Legislature and the Governor could decide to deposit the money for extra debt payments into the rainy day fund instead. Or, the Legislature and the Governor could make smaller extra debt payments and put the rest of the money into the rainy day fund.
Proposal
Save More in the Rainy Day Fund. Proposition 2 requires the state to make deposits into the rainy day fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of 10 percent of General Fund taxes). In addition, the state would make even larger deposits in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high, like when the stock market is booming.
Extend and Expand Extra Debt Payments. Proposition 2 also requires the state to make extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of through 2030). These debt payments would be the same as the amount initially deposited into the rainy day fund each year. In addition, the amount set aside for extra debt payments could be used for an expanded set of purposes. Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.
Change How Rainy Day Fund Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. Deposits into the rainy day fund would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out.
Change How Other Deposits Count Toward the State Appropriations Limit. The state has an account to set aside funds when revenues are surging. By setting these funds aside, the state can avoid overspending when revenue estimates are particularly uncertain. Under Proposition 2, deposits into this account also would not count toward the state appropriations limit. Instead, the money would count toward the limit when it is taken out. This exclusion could not be larger than 10 percent of General Fund taxes in each year.
Fiscal Effects
Budget Reserves Would Be Higher. By continuing to require deposits into the rainy day fund until the balance reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes, the state would save more over time. In addition, by depositing more money when revenues are surging, the state likely would save more in the rainy day fund in certain years. More reserves would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline.
Possibly More Debt Payments. By requiring the state to make extra debt payments through 2040, the state might make more debt payments than it would without Proposition 2.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
State budget reserves would be higher.

Pro
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

California’s tax revenue is volatile and relies heavily on the stock market. Supporters say raising the ceiling would allow the state to save more when the economy is booming, building a stronger reserve for economic downturns.

Opponents say the state’s reserves can be used by politicians as a “slush fund,” and argue the measure would allow lawmakers to withhold more tax revenue without triggering the spending limit so as to avoid refunds to taxpayers.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democrats in the state Legislature placed Proposition 2 on the November ballot to give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more in the state budget than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration.
Advertisement
Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers. More recent carve-outs in the law also allow leaders to direct excess funds to infrastructure and local government.
The limit applies to most other appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the “rainy day” fund and other reserves.
California voters also have capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund at 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short-term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
In effect, the measure would allow the governor and the Legislature to put more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid triggering rebates.
Advertisement
For example, if the spending limit is $400 billion for the year, and revenue hits $410 billion, the measure would give lawmakers the option to deposit the $10 billion above the spending limit into the rainy day fund, direct the money to infrastructure or give it to local governments, instead of returning the funding to taxpayers and increasing funding for schools.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Newsom, legislative Democrats and the California Democratic Party say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during a recession or stock market crash.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Reform California, a political action committee started by state Sen. Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego), and legislative Republicans argue the proposal will allow Democrats to spend more money and hold on to revenue that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for deposits into a savings account to count as spending under state law.
California’s budget revenue also is vulnerable to dramatic and at times unpredictable swings from year to year based on stock market activity. Newsom has said the state should have more flexibility during times of surplus to deposit money into the reserve accounts that lawmakers could then use during deficits to prevent big cuts to social services.
Advertisement
Statewide voters originally adopted the constitutional spending limit during an antitax wave in the late 1970s. Subsequent changes weakened the measure with exemptions to the limit for different kinds of appropriations, such as spending on infrastructure, and made it easier for lawmakers to avoid exceeding the limit and triggering rebates.
Revenue last exceeded the Gann Limit in 2021 when the pandemic left California with a predicted tax surplus of about $75 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-05-10/gavin-newsom-new-stimulus-checks-californians-rent-assistance). As he campaigned against a failed recall, the governor set aside about $11.8 billion in cash rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-31/state-stimulus-checks-arrive-as-california-voters-cast-ballots-recall-election) for middle class and low-income residents under a program he called the “Golden State Stimulus.” The Newsom administration predicted a historic surplus of nearly $100 billion (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-05-13/california-budget-surplus-swells-to-97-billion-under-newsom-new-plan) the next year.

Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters In summary Proponents say Prop. 2 would allow the state to shore up its reserves for an economic downturn. Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. The following is a list of statewide measures that have qualified for the ballot. For those measures that are currently attempting to qualify, see the Initiative and Referendum Qualification Status (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status) page.
For initiative measures that are eligible for the ballot, see the Eligible Statewide Initiative Measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures) page. An eligible initiative measure is one in which the required number of signatures have been submitted to and verified by the county elections officials. Eligible initiative measures will become qualified for the ballot on the 131st day prior to the next Statewide General Election unless withdrawn by the proponents prior to its qualification by the Secretary of State.
For information on the campaign committees that have organized to support or oppose propositions and ballot measures on the statewide ballot, see the Propositions and Ballot Measures Campaign Finance Activity (http://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Measures/) page.
November 3, 2026, Statewide Ballot Measures
Proposition 1
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm)
Proposition 2
Increases State's Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2/index.htm)
Proposition 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm)
Proposition 4
Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm)
Proposition 5
Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/index.htm)
Proposition 37
Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/index.htm)
Proposition 38
Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm)
Proposition 39
Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment. (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/index.htm)

What it does.
Raises the cap on the state's main reserve from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes and keeps deposits going until it's full, with bigger deposits in years when capital gains are high.
It also extends required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and changes how reserve deposits count toward the state's constitutional spending limit.

No new tax.
The state would hold more money in reserve.
What's easy to miss.
The spending-limit change is the real dispute.
Under current law, revenue above the limit can trigger taxpayer rebates and extra school payments.
Prop 2 says reserve deposits don't count toward the limit until the money is spent.
Opponents argue this makes rebates less likely.

# Proposition 2 — Doubles the State’s “Rainy Day Fund” and Lets Sacramento Sidestep Constitutional Spending Limits
*Increases the slush fund that Sacramento uses to finance such exotic programs as healthcare for illegal immigrants.*
Proposition 2 would raise the cap on the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — commonly called the rainy day fund — from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue.
It would also exclude deposits into that account from the state’s constitutional spending limit (known as the Gann Limit, which voters established through Proposition 4 in 1979).
This means that, if Proposition 2 is approved by voters, the state will have a larger rainy day fund, and that the Gann limit would not apply to spending from that account.

#### YES on Prop. 2 : Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes
California maintains a Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), a “rainy day fund” that can be used for essential services and to pay down debt during budgetary emergencies.
Currently, the state can authorize contributing up to 10% of its General Fund tax revenue to the BSA each year.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean California gets to make the maximum contribution, even if it wants to.
Contributions are constrained by “the Gann Limit,” a constitutional amendment enacted by 1970s antitax reactionaries that caps the share of tax revenue state legislators are allowed to spend in a given year, based on inflation and population growth.
Prop.
2 would amend the state constitution to both increase the percentage of General Fund tax revenue that California can contribute to its BSA from 10% to 20% *and* exempt these contributions from the Gann Limit.
This would allow the state to build a rainy day fund capable of safeguarding public services in an increasingly volatile national economy.

Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature this summer via Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Proposition 2 asks voters to approve changes to the state budget process.
On its face, it doesn’t seem too bad and the title given to it for the ballot is seemingly innocuous, “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
As the title and summary suggest, passage of Prop.
2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues.
The General Fund is the state’s main spending account.
...
Enter the 2026 Prop.
2, which would enable some of the worst behavior of the Legislature, including its practice of borrowing from other state funds, by expanding the types of debts that would count as lawful uses of that money and extending that authorization through 2040.

*Increases the slush fund that Sacramento uses to finance such exotic programs as healthcare for illegal immigrants.*
Proposition 2 would raise the cap on the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — commonly called the rainy day fund — from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue.

This means that, if Proposition 2 is approved by voters, the state will have a larger rainy day fund, and that the Gann limit would not apply to spending from that account.

Proposition 2 would change the rules around California's state budget reserves and payments toward certain debts, increasing the amount held in the state's rainy day fund.

A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.

#### YES on Prop. 2 : Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes
California maintains a Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), a “rainy day fund” that can be used for essential services and to pay down debt during budgetary emergencies.
Currently, the state can authorize contributing up to 10% of its General Fund tax revenue to the BSA each year.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean California gets to make the maximum contribution, even if it wants to.
Contributions are constrained by “the Gann Limit,” a constitutional amendment enacted by 1970s antitax reactionaries that caps the share of tax revenue state legislators are allowed to spend in a given year, based on inflation and population growth.
Prop.
2 would amend the state constitution to both increase the percentage of General Fund tax revenue that California can contribute to its BSA from 10% to 20% *and* exempt these contributions from the Gann Limit.
This would allow the state to build a rainy day fund capable of safeguarding public services in an increasingly volatile national economy.

## Proposition 2: Increases California's rainy day fund
Proposition 2 would change the rules around California's state budget reserves and payments toward certain debts, increasing the amount held in the state's rainy day fund.

#### YES on Prop. 2 : Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes
California maintains a Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), a “rainy day fund” that can be used for essential services and to pay down debt during budgetary emergencies.
Currently, the state can authorize contributing up to 10% of its General Fund tax revenue to the BSA each year.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean California gets to make the maximum contribution, even if it wants to.
Contributions are constrained by “the Gann Limit,” a constitutional amendment enacted by 1970s antitax reactionaries that caps the share of tax revenue state legislators are allowed to spend in a given year, based on inflation and population growth.
Prop.
2 would amend the state constitution to both increase the percentage of General Fund tax revenue that California can contribute to its BSA from 10% to 20% *and* exempt these contributions from the Gann Limit.
This would allow the state to build a rainy day fund capable of safeguarding public services in an increasingly volatile national economy.

#### YES on Prop. 2 : Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes
California maintains a Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), a “rainy day fund” that can be used for essential services and to pay down debt during budgetary emergencies.
Currently, the state can authorize contributing up to 10% of its General Fund tax revenue to the BSA each year.
But that doesn’t necessarily mean California gets to make the maximum contribution, even if it wants to.
Contributions are constrained by “the Gann Limit,” a constitutional amendment enacted by 1970s antitax reactionaries that caps the share of tax revenue state legislators are allowed to spend in a given year, based on inflation and population growth.
Prop.
2 would amend the state constitution to both increase the percentage of General Fund tax revenue that California can contribute to its BSA from 10% to 20% *and* exempt these contributions from the Gann Limit.
This would allow the state to build a rainy day fund capable of safeguarding public services in an increasingly volatile national economy.

## Proposition 2: Increases California's rainy day fund
Proposition 2 would change the rules around California's state budget reserves and payments toward certain debts, increasing the amount held in the state's rainy day fund.
The reserve fund is intended to help the state maintain essential services during economic downturns, when tax revenues may fall.
A yes vote would change how the state saves money and pays down debt, resulting in higher reserves and requiring additional debt payments for a longer period.
A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters, including Newsom and Becerra, say the measure would better protect funding for education, healthcare and public safety during economic downturns.
No formal opposition was submitted against the measure, though some critics argue that it could limit taxpayer rebates and weaken the effect of the state's constitutional spending limit.

PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact : State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters : CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents : None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
CON
Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

# CA Prop 2
## Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
Increases the maximum balance of the state’s rainy day reserves from 10% to 20%, changes how deposits and withdrawals from the account are calculated and authorized, exempts deposits from state spending caps, and expands mandatory repayment of certain debts and unfunded liabilities.
### SPUR's Recommendation
Given the volatile nature of California’s tax revenue structure, adequate reserve requirements are necessary to avoid severe service reductions during economic downturns.
The proposed measure would better manage this boom-and-bust cycle by requiring greater savings during good times to avoid deeper reductions during bad ones — when public safety-net services are most needed.
##### Vote YES
## What Prop. 2 Would Do
Proposition 2 would modify California’s Budget Stabilization Account (the state’s rainy day fund) to
- Increase the maximum reserve balance from 10% to 20% of the state’s annual general fund revenues.
- Require additional revenue deposits to increase the reserve and repay certain state long-term debts during periods of extraordinary revenue growth.
- Expand the definition of long-term debts eligible for repayment from the reserve and extend these requirements from 2030 to 2040.

## Proposition 2: Increases California's rainy day fund
Proposition 2 would change the rules around California's state budget reserves and payments toward certain debts, increasing the amount held in the state's rainy day fund.
The reserve fund is intended to help the state maintain essential services during economic downturns, when tax revenues may fall.
A yes vote would change how the state saves money and pays down debt, resulting in higher reserves and requiring additional debt payments for a longer period.
A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters, including Newsom and Becerra, say the measure would better protect funding for education, healthcare and public safety during economic downturns.
No formal opposition was submitted against the measure, though some critics argue that it could limit taxpayer rebates and weaken the effect of the state's constitutional spending limit.

# Proposition 2 : Larger state rainy day fund
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 2 would change the State Constitution so the state keeps saving in its main rainy day fund until the fund equals 20% of General Fund taxes, up from 10% today, and saves more in years when revenue from investment gains is very high.
It would also extend required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and stop counting rainy day fund deposits toward the state spending limit until the money is taken out.

#### Reserves
This means that money is saved instead of being spent on public programs during these periods of time.
When the economy gets worse and revenues decline, the state uses reserves to help maintain spending on public programs.
Reserves help the state avoid some spending cuts, tax increases, and borrowing to balance the budget.
Currently, the state has about $20 billion in reserves that can be used for any public program.
***State Constitution Requires the State to Save Money in the “Rainy Day Fund.”*** The State Constitution requires the state to deposit 0.75 percent of General Fund tax revenues in the state’s main rainy day fund, which is called the Budget Stabilization Account, each year.
Money in the rainy day fund can be used for any state program.
In addition, the state must put more money into the rainy day fund in years when revenue from taxes on investment gains is higher than normal.
During a budget emergency, the state can stop making deposits and/or take money out of the rainy day fund.
***Savings Are No Longer Required Once the Rainy Day Fund Reaches a Certain Level.*** Once money in the rainy day fund reaches 10 percent of General Fund taxes, the state is no longer required to make additional deposits.

## Proposition 2: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment
### Summary
Proposition 2 was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The amendment was introduced on June 25, 2026 and it passed the state Assembly by a vote of 59-8, with 12 not voting.
It passed the state Senate by a vote of 29-2, with nine not voting.
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would amend the State Constitution by changing California’s rainy day fund rules to build larger reserves and better protect public services during economic downturns and other budget emergencies.
Specifically, it would require the state to make deposits into the fund until it reaches 20 percent of General Fund taxes (instead of the current 10 percent of General Fund taxes).
It would also expand the types of state debt that can be repaid with General Fund money set aside each year and require the extra debt payments through 2040 (instead of the current date of 2030).
In addition, Prop.
2 would change how certain reserves are treated under the state spending cap, or “Gann Limit,” making it easier to save more money when revenues are strong.
The Legislature placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot through Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20.

## What is a state ballot measure?

The November 8, 2022, General Election ballot includes the following types of ballot measures.
## Initiative
- Initiatives may create or change laws or amend the California Constitution
- Initiative proponents must gather petition signatures of registered voters to place an initiative measure on the ballot
- An initiative needs a majority of the votes cast to pass
## Referendum
- A referendum is a measure that attempts to reject a law adopted by the Legislature
...
- If voters cast more NO votes than YES votes, the law is rejected.
If voters cast more YES votes, the law becomes law
## Legislative Constitutional Amendment
An amendment to the California Constitution proposed by the Legislature requires:
- Approval by a two-thirds vote of each house of the Legislature
- A majority of the votes to pass and become law

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund).
